title: Stopping distance & road safety
examples: What is the difference between thinking distance and braking distance?
How does the road surface affect stopping distance?
Can I reduce my stopping distance by changing my speed?

explain.say: Today we will learn about stopping distance on the road. Stopping distance is the total distance a car travels to stop. It has two main parts you need to know.
First is the thinking distance. This is the distance you travel before you even press the brakes. It depends on how fast you see danger.

draw.text: Thinking Distance: See danger to react

explain.say: Next is the braking distance. This is the distance the car travels once you actually apply the brakes. It depends on the car and the road.
Speed greatly affects both distances. If you increase your speed, both your thinking and braking distances get much longer. This is a key rule.
In real life, imagine you are cycling and see a pothole. Your thinking distance is the time you notice it. Your braking distance is when you squeeze your hand brakes hard.
A common mistake is forgetting that reaction time is part of thinking distance. You must account for your own reaction time always. This is crucial for safety.

items: It is part of thinking distance
It is individual to each person

faq.q: Does the type of car matter for stopping distance?
faq.a: Yes, the mass and the braking system of the car affect the braking distance. He might ask: What affects braking distance? Or: Is it just about the tires?
asks: What is the role of the car's weight?
Does the car model change stopping distance?

faq.q: Can I reduce my thinking distance by staying calm?
faq.a: Yes, reducing stress can improve your reaction time, which shortens your thinking distance. He might ask: How do I react faster? Or: Does focus help?
asks: Is focus related to thinking distance?

faq.q: Does the weather affect the braking distance?
faq.a: Yes, wet or icy roads increase the distance needed to stop. This is because the friction between the tyres and the road is reduced. He might ask: Is rain bad for stopping? Or: What about ice?
asks: How does wet weather impact stopping?

faq.q: Is thinking distance always the same for everyone?
faq.a: No, thinking distance depends on the driver's ability to perceive danger. Fatigue or distraction will increase this distance. He might ask: Can I be distracted? Or: Does tiredness count?

faq.q: If I drive slower, do I only need less braking distance?
faq.a: No, slowing down reduces both the thinking and the braking distances. Because the speed is a factor in both parts. He might ask: Is it just braking? Or: Does speed affect both parts?
asks: Is stopping distance only about brakes?

facts: Stopping distance is the sum of thinking distance and braking distance.
Speed has a significant impact on both thinking and braking distances.
Road conditions, like wet surfaces, reduce friction and increase stopping distance.
Reaction time is the time taken to notice and begin to react to a hazard.

quiz.say: If a car travels at a higher speed, what happens to its total stopping distance?

options.show: The thinking distance increases, but the braking distance decreases.
options.say: The thinking distance increases, but the braking distance decreases.

options.show: Only the thinking distance changes, not the braking distance.
options.say: Only the thinking distance changes, not the braking distance.

options.show: The stopping distance stays the same.
options.say: The stopping distance stays the same.

quiz.why: Because both the thinking and the braking distances increase as speed increases.

wrong.0: This is wrong because braking distance also increases with speed due to physics.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the physical stopping process (braking) also depends on speed.
wrong.3: This is wrong because speed directly affects the required stopping distance.

quiz.say: If the road surface is covered in ice, which distance is most affected?
quiz.why: Ice reduces the friction between the tyres and the road, making it harder to stop.

wrong.1: While distraction is a factor, the ice primarily affects the physical stopping action.
wrong.2: The effect of low friction is most pronounced during the actual braking phase.
wrong.3: The physical act of stopping, which is braking, is what is compromised by ice.
